summary: TeleportXR is a session protocol, not a document format. A server runs the live simulation and holds the truth of it; each client receives only the partial, temporary slice of state it needs right now. Three transports run in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC data channels and media tracks for real-time data and audio, and plain HTTP for static assets. Its own documentation states that Teleport has no file format and that the Teleport network is part of the Internet but not part of the Web. It is by some distance the most completely specified subject in this group at the session layer, and it is the only one here that states its unit: linear units are metres, and handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. Between 2026-06-16 and 2026-09-03 the identity gap that used to define this subject was largely filled, in the reference implementations first and the specification second. An avatar offer may now carry the address of a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset URL; the server verifies Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON, gates each facet against the subject's own consent records with default-deny, and returns a structured receipt. Separately the connect message's identity member, still documented as an opaque string, is implemented as a structured identity with three trust levels and a challenge-response that binds an OpenID Connect token to a client-held key. Three cautions. The chapter that would specify the manifest mechanism, avatar_manifest, is referenced from three places and is not in the public repository. Verification is explicitly not proof of the bearer's right to the document, and only trust tier zero is supported. And watch the word Node: a TeleportXR node is a changing object inside a live stream with no URL, which is not what the same word means in a world-addressing API.

coverage.note: Three layers in parallel: a WebSocket for signalling, WebRTC by default for real-time streams with optional legacy SRT and EFP, and HTTP or HTTPS for static assets. Reliable payloads must work over either the WebSocket or the WebRTC reliable channel and receivers must accept both for the whole session. One caution for an implementer: the normative channel table says five SCTP data channels and three other places in the same documentation set say six, so the count is not settled in the text; channels are matched by label, and five labels are defined.

coverage.note: Handedness and vertical axis are negotiated rather than assumed. The client declares its native axes in the handshake, the server publishes the axes its scene is authored in, and every server-to-client packet carrying geometry is already converted into the client's standard. coverage.note: This is the row that changed most since 2026-06-16, and it is the single most consequential change in the subject. An avatar offer may now name a signed Universal Manifest instead of a bare asset address, and the server reads the asset address out of the verified manifest. The reference server ships the resolver, verifies Signature Profile A (Ed25519 over RFC 8785 canonical JSON with the signature member removed), gates every facet by the subject's own consent records with default-deny, caches on the manifest's own expiry rather than the HTTP response, and returns a structured receipt to the client saying what it did with the document. Two limits are stated by the implementers themselves and both matter: only trust tier zero, signature-only, is actually verified, and verification deliberately does not check that the manifest's subject is the client presenting it, so a verified manifest is authentic but not proof of the bearer's right to it. The older empty proof registry is still there in the signalling document, and mid-session revocation remains real.

Both reference servers now treat that bare string as a legacy shape and accept an object with a provider, an issuer, a subject and a display name, sorted into three trust levels: anonymous, asserted, and verified. coverage.note: This row was scored none and that is no longer true. The reference server now has a credential verification registry keyed by credential type, with a named list of the schemes a server might accept: an OpenID Connect identity token, a plain OAuth2 access token, a W3C verifiable credential or decentralized identifier proof, and a SAML assertion. One of the four is implemented; the rest are left to host applications. The implemented one is careful: the identity token is bound to a long-lived client key by putting the key's thumbprint in the token's nonce, and a live challenge-response proves the presenter holds that key, so a token captured by one server cannot be replayed at another. TeleportXR still defines no credential format of its own. An earlier claim in this row, that the words consent, trust, permission, provenance, encryption and credential were all absent from the project, no longer holds and is withdrawn.
